author: ROBERT LANGEN Staff Reporter
title: Women in Law club provides professional development for aspiring lawyers - NewsBreak
text:
By ROBERT LANGEN Staff Reporter ,
7 hours ago Purdue’s Women in Law club is working to make the path to law school more transparent for students by providing prospective lawyers with resources and a community.
The organization, founded in 2024, aims to “create a strong network of women who are interested in entering the legal field,” said Hadley Beard, the club’s president and a junior double majoring in law and society and organizational leadership.
Beard said the goal of the club is to create a space where members can learn about the legal profession, build confidence, and work toward increased representation in law.
Women in Law meets every other Tuesday at 6:30 p.m. in WALC B058, Beard said. The club alternates between guest-speaker and activity-based meetings, giving members exposure to legal careers while also focusing on professional development and community-building.
Women in Law club stickers were distributed at their latest meeting on Tuesday. Robert Langen | Staff Reporter “What you saw tonight was a guest speaker,” Beard said. “And then, we’ll go to an activity… We’ll do professional building things, like resume building, LinkedIn, how to network… and then we’ll also do things that are just fun, like mocktails and murder mysteries or vision boards.”
This week’s meeting featured guest speaker Anastasia Sichuga-Florea, a Purdue graduate and a member of the organization’s founding board, who is now at Vanderbilt and in her first year of law school. Sichuga-Florea said Women in Law was created in response to a need she and her peers saw on campus.
“We felt like there needed to be space for women who wanted to pursue a legal career,” Sichuga-Florea said.
Sichuga-Florea said the club helped her during the law school application process by connecting her with speakers and giving her a clearer view of what law school involves.
“We had a lot of guest speakers, either current or former (…) judges, professors, and really people involved in legal backgrounds,” Sichuga-Florea said. She continued by saying that board involvement helped her understand the application process while she was applying herself.
“At the time I was on board, I was applying to law school. So I had a first-hand perspective (…) and could also talk about and share with members.”
Beard said that Women in Law is open to all students, including men, and students across majors, including STEM and business. Students can attend meetings at any point in the semester, but those who want official membership have to pay annual dues, she said.
Dues are $25 for the academic year, Beard said. Paying dues is what allows students to list formal membership on a resume and take part in additional opportunities the club shares outside of meetings.
Looking ahead, the club has several upcoming events, including a guest speaker scheduled for Feb. 24. The speaker is a labor and employment attorney.
Another meeting, planned for March 10, will focus on professional attire through an interactive “professional fashion show,” where members will model different dress codes and discuss what is and is not appropriate in professional settings, Beard said. The activity will also include trivia, with a prize intended to help a member add a professional item to their wardrobe.
Anastasia Sichuga-Florea, a Purdue alumna and former club member, returned to speak about her experiences. Robert Langen | Staff Reporter The club is also planning a law school visit on March 3, where members will travel to Indiana University Maurer School of Law for a daylong experience. The visit is expected to include opportunities, such as sitting in on classes and engaging with law school faculty and students.
For students considering law school, Sichuga-Florea said her advice was to prepare early by building comfort with reading, writing, and legal-style analysis.
“The best thing that you can do is take any law-related classes that Purdue has,” she said, pointing to courses that involve reading cases and learning to discuss them. She encourages students to prioritize writing-intensive classes, noting that law school is “reading and writing heavy.”
Women in Law is meant to be a place where students can become familiar with the legal track and realize they don’t have to navigate it alone, Sichuga-Florea said.
